title: Name an organiser by what it asks
statement: Don't give learners a branded name for a graphic organiser to remember; name it by its function and say what it asks in plain question language.
example: One unit resolved a branded organiser name by calling the tool a plain five-part chart.
detail: Curriculum feedback on a grade 3 reading course found that naming an organiser with a branded frame name just gives students one more label to remember, and asked for plain questions about what it is for. The rule went into the course's generation contract, which bans branded frames; an authored grade 4 lesson still used one, and its unit's sign-off resolved it by naming the tool by its function (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/video/u1-course-plan-notes.md`, lines 278-280). Procedures are treated the other way: the course names them on purpose, as tools the child carries.
against: Procedures, unlike organisers, are named on purpose in the same course: "a child who has watched FIND four times without once hearing it called FIND has been given four demonstrations and no tool." (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/pedagogy-and-lesson-structure.md`, lines 343-345); and an authored grade 4 lesson used a named frame until its unit's sign-off renamed it (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/content-and-copy.md`, lines 198-199).

evidence.quote: **Rule.** Do not give the child a label to remember. Say what the frame asks.
"Naming the organizer the 'Adaptation Frame' just gives students one more label to remember. Use plain question language instead ('what problem is the animal solving? how does it survive?')."
Contract §A2.2 bans branded frames such as "the Adaptation Frame". The signoff resolved this for U1 by naming the tool by function, a plain five-part chart.
